He said to them, “Into whom, then, were you baptized?” They said, “We were baptized into John.”
Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
When Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in other languages and prophesied.
There were twelve men in all.
He entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, discussing and persuading them about the kingdom of God.

But when some became hard-hearted and refused to listen, speaking against the Way before the crowd, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples from them. He spoke with them daily in the school of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that everyone living in Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.
God was performing great miracles through Paul's hands.
People even took handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched his body and laid them on the sick. Their illnesses ceased, and the evil spirits came out of them.
Some traveling Jewish exorcists tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, "We command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims."
There was a Jewish chief priest named Sceva who had seven sons who were doing this.
The evil spirit answered them, "I know Jesus, and I am acquainted with Paul, but who are you?"
The man who had the evil spirit leaped on them, overpowered all seven of them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was honored.
Many of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring what they had done.
Many who had practiced magic also brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. They calculated their value and found that they were worth fifty thousand pieces of silver.
In this way the word of the Lord grew, became firmly established, and gained strength.
After these things were completed, Paul resolved in the spirit to travel through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem. He said, “After I go there, I must also see Rome.”
He sent to Macedonia for two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, while he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
At that time a great disturbance arose concerning the Way.
For a silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver idols of Artemis, provided a great deal of business for the craftsmen.
He gathered everyone who worked at this trade and said to them, "Fellow craftsmen, you know that we make our living from this business.
You see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, this man Paul has persuaded and turned away a large crowd, saying that things made with human hands are not gods.

Not only is this trade in danger of being destroyed and taken out of our hands, but people will also stop esteeming the temple of the great Artemis, and she will be brought down from her greatness—she whom all Asia and the inhabited world worship."
When they heard this, they were filled with anger and shouted, "Great is Artemis of Ephesus!"
The whole city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who traveled with Paul.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Some of the officials who were his friends also sent word to him, pleading with him not to enter the theater.
They were shouting, each one saying something different, for the crowd was confused, and most of them did not know why they had gathered.
The Jews pushed forward someone from the crowd named Alexander. Alexander motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defense before the crowd.
But when they realized that he was a Jew, everyone shouted with one voice for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of Ephesus!"
After the city clerk had quieted the crowd, he said to them, “People of Ephesus, who does not know that the city of Ephesus serves the great Artemis and Zeus?
“Since these things are clear, you ought to calm yourselves and do nothing rashly.”
For you have brought these men here, although they have neither robbed temples nor spoken against your goddess.
So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a complaint against them, there are court sessions and proconsuls. Let them bring charges against them.
“But if you are seeking something else, it will be settled in the regular assembly.”
For we are in danger of being charged over today's disturbance, since there is no cause for it that we can give an account of.
After saying these things, he dismissed the crowd.
After the disturbance had ended, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye to them, and left to go to Macedonia.
After traveling through those regions and encouraging them with many words, he came to Greece.
After he had spent three months there, the Jews plotted against him as he was about to sail to Syria. He decided to return through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius of Derbe and Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus from Ephesus.
These men went ahead and waited for us in Troas.
We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and reached them in Troas within five days. We stayed there seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered to break bread, Paul spoke with them. He was leaving the next day, and he continued speaking until midnight.
There were many lamps burning in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the windowsill, overcome by deep sleep. As Paul spoke, sleep weighed on him more heavily, and he fell down from the third story. They picked him up dead.
Paul went down, bent over him, and embraced him. They said to them, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is still in him.”
After he went upstairs, he broke the bread and ate. He continued talking with them until dawn, and then he left.
They brought the young man back alive, and he comforted them greatly.
We went ahead to the ship and sailed to Tharsos [?], intending to take Paul aboard there. This was what he had arranged with us, since he himself intended to travel on foot.
When he met us at Tharsos [?], we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
The next day we sailed from there and came opposite Chios. The following day we put in at Samos, and after staying at Trogyllium, we came to Miletus the next day.
For Paul had decided not to put in at Ephesus, so that he would not spend time in Asia. He was hurrying to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, if he could.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the church.
When they came to him, he said to them, “Brothers, you yourselves know how I spent all this time with you, from the first day I set foot in Asia,
serving the Lord with complete humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
I did not withhold anything that would benefit you, failing to tell you about it or to teach you publicly and in your homes.
I testified to both Jews and Greeks about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now, look: bound by the Spirit, I am going up to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there.
But the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying, “Chains and hardships await you in Jerusalem.”

But I do not consider my life worth anything compared with completing my course and the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify to the Jews and the Greeks about the good news of God’s grace.
Now, then, look: I know that from now on none of you among whom I went about preaching the kingdom of Jesus will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you today that I am innocent of everyone’s blood.
For I did not hold back from telling you the whole plan of God.

So pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as overseers, to shepherd the church of the Lord, which he acquired for himself through his own blood.
I know that after I leave, fierce wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.
And men will arise from among you yourselves, speaking distorted things to draw the disciples away after them.
Therefore stay alert, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never stopped teaching each one of you with tears.
Now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you the inheritance among all those who are holy.
I have not coveted any silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands provided for my needs and for those who were with me.

In everything I have shown you that you must work hard in this way and support those who are weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
When Paul had said these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
Everyone began weeping bitterly, and they threw their arms around Paul’s neck and kissed him.
They were especially distressed over what he had said: “You will not see my face again.” Then they accompanied him to the ship.
When we had parted from them and set sail, we sailed straight to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara, and afterward to Myra.
And when we found a ship bound for Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail.
When we reached Cyprus, we left it on our left and sailed to Syria. We came to Tyre, for the ship was to unload there.
And when we found the disciples, we stayed with them for seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
When those days were over, we left and went on our way. They all accompanied us, with their wives and children, to the outskirts of the city. And we knelt down on the shore and prayed.
We said goodbye to one another and boarded the ship, while they returned to their homes.
We sailed from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais. After greeting the brothers, we stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.
He had four daughters who were virgins and who prophesied.
After we had stayed there for many days, a prophet named Agabus came from Judea.

When he came to us, he took Paul's belt and tied his own feet and hands with it. He said, “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt in this way and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, we and the people there begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
But when he would not be persuaded, we stopped speaking and said, “May the Lord's will be done.”
After these days, we got ready and traveled up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea came with us and took us to stay with a long-standing disciple from Cyprus named Mnason.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully.
The next day, Paul went with us to see James, and some elders were gathered with him.
After greeting them, he sat down and recounted, one by one, the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they gave glory to the Lord and said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of believers there are in Judea, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have heard about you that you teach all the Jews throughout the world to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or follow his customs.
What, then, will happen? They will certainly hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men here who have taken a vow upon themselves.

Take these men and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they have heard about you is false, and that you yourself uphold the law and observe it.”

As for the Gentiles who have believed, they have nothing to say to you, for we have decided and written to them that they should keep away from sacrifices to idols, blood, dead animals, and sexual immorality.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself with them. He entered the temple, announcing the days until the completion of the purification, when a sacrifice would be offered for each of them.
When the seven days were nearly over, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd, and laid their hands on him.

They shouted, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this temple. He has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place!”
For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city and thought that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was in an uproar, and the people gathered together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, a report reached the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in turmoil.
Immediately he took some centurions and soldiers and ran down to them. When they saw the commander, the centurions, and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander approached, seized him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
The people in the crowd were shouting, each saying something different. Since he could not establish the facts because of the crowd's uproar, he ordered Paul to be taken up to the barracks.
When they reached the stairs, the soldiers had to carry him because of the crowd's violent rush.
For all the people were following him, shouting, “Remove our enemy from our midst!”
As they were about to take Paul into the barracks, he said to the commander, “May I say something to you?” He replied, “Do you know Greek?
Then you are not the Egyptian who recently started a revolt and led the four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?”
Paul said, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a renowned city. I beg you, let me speak to the people.”
When the commander gave him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the people. When a deep silence fell, he addressed them in Hebrew, saying:
“My brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make before you.”
When they heard that he was speaking to them in Hebrew, they became even quieter. And he said:

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city. At the feet of Gamaliel, I was thoroughly instructed in the law of my ancestors. I was zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding both men and women and throwing them into prisons.
The high priest and the elders can also testify to this. I received letters from them and went to Damascus to bring those who were there to Jerusalem as well, so that they would be punished.
As I was traveling and approaching Damascus at noon, a great light from heaven suddenly shone down on me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’
Those who were traveling with me saw the light and became afraid, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said, ‘Lord, what shall I do?’ He said to me, ‘Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told about everything I have appointed you to do.’
When I got up, I could no longer see because of the brightness of that light. Those who were with me led me by the hand, and I went into Damascus.
A man named Ananias, who was devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living in Damascus,
came to me and stood beside me. He said to me, ‘Saul, my brother, regain your sight.’ At that very moment I regained my sight.
He said to me, ‘The God of our ancestors has chosen you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth.
For you will be his witness before everyone to what you have seen and heard.
So now, what will you do? Get up, be baptized, wash away your sins, and call on his name.’
When I returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance.
I saw him saying to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’
I replied, ‘Lord, they know that I was the one who imprisoned those who believe in you and beat them in the synagogues.
And when the blood of Stephen, your witness, was being shed, I too stood there approving and guarding the clothes of those who were killing him.’
He said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you to Gentiles far away.’”
The crowds listened to him up to this statement. Then they raised their voices, saying, “Rid the earth of someone like this! He should not live any longer!”
As they shouted, lifted up their clothes, and threw dust into the air,
the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks. He said to beat him with whips so that he could find out why they were shouting against him like this.
When they stretched him out with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it lawful for you to beat a Roman citizen who has not been found guilty?”
When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and told him, “Be careful what you are about to do, because this man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander went to him and asked, “Are you a Roman citizen?” He answered, “Yes.”
The commander replied, “I paid a large sum of money for this citizenship.” Paul said, “But I was born with it.”
Those who were about to interrogate him immediately withdrew from him. The commander was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman citizen, because he had bound him, and he immediately untied him.
The next day, wanting to know for certain why the Jews were accusing him, he ordered the chief priests and the entire council to assemble. He brought Paul down and had him stand among them.
Paul looked intently at the council and said, “Brothers, I have lived before God with an entirely good conscience up to this day.”
The high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the law, yet you have ordered me to be struck contrary to the law.”
Those standing there said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “Brothers, I did not know that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You must not speak evil of the ruler of your people.’”

When Paul realized that one group consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, he shouted out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. I am being judged because of hope and the resurrection of the dead.”
When he said this, a dispute arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge that there is a resurrection, and that there are angels and spirits.

When a great uproar arose, some of the scribes belonging to the Pharisees’ group stood up and argued vigorously, saying, “We find nothing wrong with this man. If a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, then let us not fight against God.”
When the dispute became fierce, the commander feared that they might kill Paul. He ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night, the Lord stood beside him and said to him, “Take courage! Just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, you must also testify in the same way in Rome.”
When morning came, some of the Jews swore an oath to one another, saying, “We will neither eat nor drink until we have killed Paul.”
There were more than forty men who had made this oath.
They went to the chief priests and the elders, saying, “We have bound ourselves by an oath to one another not to taste anything until we have killed Paul.”

“We ask you to do this for us: assemble the council and tell the commander to bring him into your midst, as though you were going to question him more thoroughly about the matters he is involved in. For we are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
Paul’s sister’s son heard about their plot. He went into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander, because he has something to tell him.”
He took the young man and brought him in to the commander, saying, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man in to you, because he has something to tell you.”
The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked him, “What do you have to tell me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul into the council tomorrow, as though they were going to investigate his case more thoroughly.”

So do not listen to them. More than forty men from among them are lying in wait for him. They have sworn to one another not to eat or drink until they have killed him. Now they are ready, waiting for you to give them your consent.
The commander dismissed the young man, ordering him, “Do not tell anyone that you have informed me of these things.”
He called two of the centurions and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, along with one hundred cavalrymen and two hundred spearmen, starting at the third hour of the night.
And prepare animals for Paul to ride, so that they may bring him before Felix the governor.”
He wrote a letter in this form:
“Claudius Lysias writes to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews, who wanted to kill him. I came upon them with the troops, and when I learned that he was a Roman, I rescued him.
Wanting to know the reason for their accusation against him, I brought him before their council.
I found that they were accusing him over questions concerning their law, but there was no charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.
When I was informed of a plot that the Jews were going to carry out against this man, I immediately sent him to you, ordering his accusers to bring their case against him before you.”
So the soldiers, following the orders they had been given, took Paul during the night and brought him to Antipatris.
The next day they let the cavalrymen go on with them and returned to the barracks.
When they entered Caesarea, they gave the letter to the governor and presented Paul to him.
When the governor read it, he asked what province he was from. When he learned that he was from Cilicia,
he said, “I will hear you when your accusers also arrive.” He ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod’s headquarters.
After five days, Ananias the high priest came down with some elders and an advocate named Tertullus. They brought charges against Paul before the governor.
When Paul was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “We enjoy great peace through you, and benefits have come to this nation through your foresight.
Most excellent Felix, we are honored at all times and in every place, with great gratitude.
But so that we do not trouble you any further, I beg you, in your kindness, to hear us briefly.
For we have found this man to be a plague, stirring up unrest among all the Jews throughout the world. He is the leader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He also tried to defile the temple, and we seized him.
By questioning him yourself, you can learn about all these things of which we accuse him.”
The Jews also responded, saying that these things were so.
The governor motioned to Paul to speak, and he replied, “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I will speak in my own defense with confidence.
You can find out that it has been no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me arguing with anyone in the temple or gathering a crowd, either in their synagogues or in the city.
Nor can they substantiate the accusations they are now bringing against me.
But I confess this to you: according to the Way, which these people call a sect, I worship the God of my ancestors, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets.
I have hope in God, which these people themselves await: the resurrection that will take place for the righteous and the unrighteous.
I too have worked at this, so that I may always maintain a blameless conscience before God and other people.
After many years, I came to my nation to give alms and offer sacrifices.
While I was doing these things, some Jews from Asia found me in the temple purifying myself, without a crowd or a disturbance.
These people ought to be here and bring accusations if they have anything against me.
Otherwise, let these people themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before the council.
Unless it is because of this one statement that I shouted while standing among them: ‘I am being judged before you today because of the resurrection of the dead.’
When Felix heard these things, he postponed the matter, since he had accurate knowledge of the Way. He said, “When Lysias, the commander, comes, I will hear you.”
He ordered the centurion to guard Paul but not to make things difficult for him, and not to prevent any of his people from attending to him or visiting him.
After some days, Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul spoke about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix became afraid and replied, “Go away for now. When I find an opportunity, I will send for you.”
At the same time, he hoped that Paul would give him money so that he would release him. For this reason, he frequently sent for him and talked with him.
When Felix’s two years were completed, Porcius Festus took his place. But Felix wanted to do the Jews a favor, so he left Paul in chains.
Three days after Festus arrived in the province, he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the Jewish leaders presented their accusations against Paul to him.
They pleaded with him, asking him for the favor of sending for Paul to come to Jerusalem, while they planned an ambush to kill him along the way.
Festus therefore replied, “Paul is being held in Caesarea, and I myself will go there shortly.”
“Let those among you who have authority go down and bring accusations if there is anything wrong with this man.”
After spending eight or ten days there, he went down to Caesarea. The next day, when he sat on the judgment seat, I ordered Paul to be brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing grave and serious accusations against him that they could not prove.
Paul answered them, “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, against the temple, or against the emperor.”
Festus, wanting to do the Jews a favor, replied to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there with them before me concerning these things?”
Paul said, “I am standing before the emperor’s judgment seat. This is where I am to be tried. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know very well.”

“If I had committed a wrong or done anything deserving death, I would not refuse to die. But if I have done none of the things these people accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to the emperor.”
Then Festus, after speaking with his adviser, replied, “You have appealed to the emperor; you will go before the emperor.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to greet Festus.
After they had spent many days there, Festus told the king about Paul's case, saying, "There is a man whom Felix left in custody."
"When I went up to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought a complaint against him to me, asking that he be put to death."

"I answered them that it is not the Roman custom to hand over an accused person to be put to death before his accusers have come face to face with him and he has had an opportunity to answer the accusation."
"So when they came here, I did not delay the matter. The next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought in."
"But when his accusers stood up against him, they did not establish any charge of wrongdoing against him of the kind I had expected."
"Instead, they had disputes with him about their religion and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul said was alive."
"Since I was uncertain about how to judge these matters, I asked him whether he wanted to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial with them about these things."
"But when Paul appealed to be kept in custody for the emperor's judgment, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to the emperor."
Agrippa said to Festus, "I too would like to hear this man." He replied, "Tomorrow you will hear him."
The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the place of judgment with military commanders and wealthy men of the city. At Festus's command, Paul was brought in.
Festus said, "King Agrippa, and everyone here, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish community petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he should no longer be allowed to live."
"But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. Since he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him."

"But I have nothing definite to write to the emperor about him. That is why I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after you examine him, I may find something to write."
"For it does not seem right to me to send a prisoner without also writing down the charges against him."
Agrippa said to Paul, "You have permission to speak on your own behalf." Then Paul stretched out his hand and said:
"King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to make my defense before you today concerning everything the Jews accuse me of,"
"especially since you know all the customs and disputes of the Jews. Therefore I ask you to listen to me patiently."
"All the Jews know how I have lived since my youth among my own people in Jerusalem."
"They have known me from the beginning, and if they are willing to testify truthfully, they know that I lived according to the strict sect of my religion as a Pharisee."
"And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise God made to our ancestors."
"The twelve tribes of our people hope to attain this promise as they worship with earnest prayer night and day. It is because of this hope, O king, that the Jews accuse me."
"Why do you consider it unbelievable that God will raise the dead?"
"I myself had determined to oppose the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene as much as possible."
"And that is what I did in Jerusalem. Having received authority from the chief priests, I put many of the holy ones in prison, and I also cast my vote to put them to death."
"I punished them many times in every synagogue, forcing them to blaspheme his name. In my extreme anger against them, I pursued them even to distant cities."
I was going to Damascus with the authority I had received from the chief priests.
At noon on the road, O king, I saw a light shining from heaven, brighter than the light of the sun. It shone down on me and those traveling with me.
When we had all fallen to the ground in fear, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.”
I said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said to me, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
“But get up and stand on your feet. I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and a witness to how you have seen me and how I will appear to you.”
“I will rescue you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,”

“to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s authority to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of their sins and an inheritance among the holy ones through believing in me.”
Therefore, King Agrippa, I did not disobey the revelation that came to me from heaven.
But I preached first in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout the whole region of the Jews, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of repentance.
For this reason, the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
But I have received help from God, and I stand here to this day, bearing witness to small and great alike. I say nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen:
that Christ would suffer, that he would be the first to rise from the dead, and that he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.
While he was saying these things, Festus said to him in a loud voice, “Paul, you are mad! Your great learning has driven you mad!”
But Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus. I am speaking words of truth and sound judgment.”
“King Agrippa knows about these things, and I speak freely with him. I am convinced that none of these things is hidden from him, for this did not happen in secret.”
“King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “With a few words you are persuading me to become a Christian.”
Paul said, “I pray to God that, whether with little or much, not only you but everyone listening to me today may become as I am, except for these chains.”
When he had said these things, the king stood up, along with the governor, Bernice, and those seated beside them.
They withdrew and spoke to one another, saying, “This man has done nothing deserving death.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to the emperor.”
When it was decided that we should sail to Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, from the Augustan cohort.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was going to sail to places in Asia, and we set sail. Aristarchus, who was from Thessalonica in Macedonia, came with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends so they could care for him.
We set sail from there and sailed along the sheltered side of Cyprus because the winds were against us.
After sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found a ship from Alexandria that was going to sail to Italy, and he put us aboard it.
After we had sailed slowly for many days and had barely reached Cnidus, the wind would not let us continue, so we sailed along the sheltered side of Crete, off Salmone.
After we had barely managed to pass along its coast, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near a city called Lasea.
After much time had passed, we were in danger on the voyage because the Fast had already passed. Paul advised them.
He said, “Men, I can see that the voyage will involve hardship and great loss, not only of the ship and its cargo, but also of our lives.”
But the centurion listened to the pilot and the shipowner rather than to what Paul was saying.

Since the harbor was not suitable for spending the winter, the majority decided to leave that place to see whether we could reach a harbor in Crete called Phoenix and spend the winter there. It faces west and toward the mainland.
When the south wind began to blow, they thought that their purpose had been achieved. They set out from [?] and left Crete behind.
A little later, a violent wind called Euroclydon struck against us.
When it seized the ship, and the ship could not resist the wind, we gave way and were driven along.
We reached a place near an island called Clauda, and we could barely manage to secure the boat.
They climbed aboard it and used supports to bind the ship. Fearing that they might run aground on a shallow place, they lowered the equipment and let themselves drift.
As the storm continued to batter us severely, the next day they threw their cargo overboard.
The day after that, they threw all the ship’s equipment into the sea.
Neither the sun nor the stars appeared for several days, and a great storm was upon us. We no longer had any hope of being saved.
After they had gone a long time without eating, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete, and so avoided this hardship and loss.”
Now again I tell you to take courage, for not a single life among you will be lost, but only the ship.
For an angel of my God, whom I serve, appeared to me tonight,
saying, “Do not be afraid, Paul. You must be brought to stand before the king. And look, God has graciously granted you everyone sailing with you.”
So, men, take courage, for I believe God that it will happen just as I was told.
We must run aground on an island.
When the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven along in the Adriatic Sea, the sailors said at midnight that we were approaching land.
They lowered the sounding line and found twenty cubits of water. After a little while, they again lowered the sounding line into the water and found fifteen cubits.
Fearing that we might run aground on a rocky place, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight to come.
The sailors were trying to escape and abandon the ship. They lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they were going to drop anchors from the bow.
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay aboard the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut the boat’s ropes and let it drift away.
Until daybreak was near, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued hungry without eating anything.
So I urge you to take some food, for this is necessary for your survival. Not a single hair will fall from the head of any of you.”
After saying this, he took a loaf of bread and thanked God in front of everyone. He broke it and began to eat, giving some to us as well.
Then they all took courage and ate some food themselves.
There were seventy-six of us in all on the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the place, but they noticed a bay with a place to land. They discussed whether they could bring the ship safely in there.
They cut loose the anchors and left them hanging in the sea. At the same time, they untied the rudders, raised the foresail, and headed toward the shore with the wind blowing.
They came upon a shoal in the sea and ran the ship onto it. Its bow became firmly stuck and remained motionless, but its stern broke apart under the force of the wind.
The soldiers then planned to kill the prisoners so that none of them would swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul and stopped their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump in first and make their way to shore.
The rest were to follow, some on planks and others on objects from the ship. In this way everyone reached shore safely.
After we had reached safety, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us great kindness. They lit a fire and welcomed us because of the cold wind and the rain.
Paul gathered a large quantity of sticks and threw them onto the fire. A snake came out because of the heat and fastened its mouth onto his hand.

When the local people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “This man is certainly a murderer. Although he escaped from the sea, the punishment he deserves has not allowed him to live.”
But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They watched him, expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down and die. But after watching him for a long time and seeing that nothing bad had happened to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
There were estates in that area belonging to the island’s chief official, whose name was Publius. He welcomed us for three days and showed us great hospitality.
Publius’s father was lying sick with a fever and an intestinal illness. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hand on him, and healed him.
After this happened, the other people on the island who had illnesses came to him, and he healed them.
They gave us great honors, and when we were about to sail, we loaded what we needed.
After three months, we sailed on a ship from Alexandria that had been moored at the island. It bore the emblem of the Dioscuri, the Twin Brothers.
We landed at Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
From there we sailed and reached Rhegium. After one day, a south wind began to blow, and on the second day we reached Puteoli.
We found some brothers there, and they urged us to stay with them for seven days. And so we went to Rome.
When the brothers there heard about us, they came out from the Three Taverns as far as the Forum of Appius to meet us. When Paul saw them, he took courage and thanked God.
When we entered Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the soldiers. But he allowed Paul to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days, he called together the Jewish leaders and said to them, “My brothers, although I did nothing against our people or the customs established by our ancestors, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
After questioning me, they wanted to release me because they found no grounds in my case for a death sentence.
But when the Jews opposed me, I was forced to appeal to the emperor, though I had no intention of bringing an accusation against my own nation.
For this reason, then, I asked to see you and speak with you, for I am bound with this chain because of the hope of Israel.
They then said to him, “We have neither received letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers come and reported or said anything bad about you.
But we ask to hear from you what you think, for we have been told that this sect is spoken against everywhere.”

They arranged a day with him, and a large number came to him at the place where he was staying. He spoke with them, testifying about the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening.
Some were persuaded by what he said, but others did not believe.
They left, disagreeing with one another, after Paul had said this one thing to them: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly to your ancestors through Isaiah the prophet:
He said, “Go to this people and tell them: ‘You will indeed hear, but you will not understand; you will indeed see, but you will not perceive.’”

‘For this people’s heart has grown dull, and they have become hard of hearing with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I heal them.’
Let it therefore be known to you that this salvation from God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.”
Omission.
Paul spent two whole years living in a place he had rented, and he welcomed everyone who came to him.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness, without hindrance. The Acts of the Apostles.
